parsed.assessment_summary: This paper presents an in-depth cost-effectiveness analysis of two charities, Friendship Bench and StrongMinds, which deliver lay-delivered talk psychotherapy in Africa. The core metric is the cost-effectiveness of interventions and charities based on their impact on subjective wellbeing, measured in terms of wellbeing-adjusted life years (WELLBYs). The analysis uses three sources of evidence: (1) a meta-analysis of 84 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of psychotherapy in low and middle-income countries (LMICs); (2) RCTs of programs related to the charities (4 for Friendship Bench and 1 for StrongMinds); and (3) Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) pre-post data from the charities themselves. The authors estimate the initial effect and duration, adjust the total effect to account for internal and external validity concerns, and estimate household spillovers. They then calculate a final effect estimate for each charity by combining the three estimates from different evidence sources, using informed subjective weights, and calculate the cost-effectiveness. Several updates were performed in this version of the analysis, including the extraction of additional small sample studies, a second risk of bias evaluation, the inclusion of a recent working paper, an updated weighting system, the addition of charity monitoring and evaluation (M&E) pre-post results as an additional source of evidence, site visits, and updated program implementation details. The authors assess the overall quality of evidence using a stringent GRADE-adapted criteria. Key limitations include the very low attendance/dosage with Friendship Bench, the fact that the only RCT of the StrongMinds programme (Baird et al., 2024) is only partially relevant, and the subjectivity involved in weighting the different evidence sources. They find both charities are cost effective, though this depends greatly on what weighting one gives to the Baird et al paper.
